title: Coming back after a lapse
hookLine: a Sikh who breaks rehat can return through penance and a fresh start

lines: A LETTER: YOU ARE NOT OUR GURU.
cards: A folded piece of paper. On it, a few lines that say, in effect: you are not our Guru, and we are not your Sikhs.
Sikh tradition tells of a band of men from the Majha region who wrote a letter like that during the long siege of Anandpur, signed it, handed it to Guru Gobind Singh, and went home.
The word for that letter is bedava, a disclaimer. Tradition says the Guru kept it. You've met the penance the five set when the code is broken.

teach.b: Here's how the story is told. At home, the men are met with shame instead of welcome. A woman named Mai Bhago, whom you've met before on this path, won't let it rest.
Tradition says she rode out with them, back toward the Guru, and they caught up with his pursuers near a pool called Khidrana. They fought there, and they fell.

When the Guru came over the field, he found one of them, Mahan Singh, still breathing, and lifted his head into his lap. The dying man asked for one thing: tear up the letter. And the Guru took out the bedava and tore it.

Sikhs remember those men as the Mukte, the liberated; the place is called Muktsar, and they're remembered in the Ardas, the prayer said at the close of Sikh gatherings. Now set the code beside the story.

teach.h: THE CODE: ADMIT, ACCEPT, BEGIN AGAIN.
teach.b: The Rehat Maryada says, in paraphrase, that a Sikh who breaks the rehat should come before the five, admit it plainly, accept the penance they set, and, where amrit has been broken, take it again.
Then the person begins fresh. As the code lays it out, the procedure is a way back in. The story says the same thing in another key.
The men didn't come back by arguing they'd been right. They came back, and gave everything. The paper that said we are not your Sikhs wasn't filed away as evidence.

how: A Sikh who has broken the rehat appears before five amritdhari Sikhs, admits the lapse, and accepts a penance (tankhah); where amrit has been broken, it is taken again. The story of the Mukte of Muktsar is told as a picture of return.

games.q: what does “coming back after a lapse” mean?
o: paying a fine to the jathedar to clear your name
being barred from the gurdwara for the rest of your life
admitting it before the five, and starting fresh

games.q: inside the return: tap the pairs.
p: rode the men back toward the Guru
asked for the letter to be torn
set the penance in the code

s: in the code, a Sikh who breaks rehat can never come back
the code sets a way back: come before the five, admit it, accept the penance, and begin again.
in the story, the Guru tore up the letter
tradition says Mahan Singh, dying, asked for it, and the Guru tore the bedava.
the men returned by arguing they'd been right
the story doesn't give them a speech. they came back, and they gave everything.

games.q: you're the Guru, holding the letter that says 'you are not our Guru'. one of the men who signed it is dying in your lap and asks for one thing. what do you do?
o: keep the letter as a record of what they did.
read it aloud to the others.
games.why: tradition says the Guru tore the bedava. the men are remembered as the Mukte, the liberated, and the place is called Muktsar.

practice: Bring to mind someone who drifted away, from you, a family, a team, a friendship or a faith community, whether they left loudly or just stopped coming.

Hold them without rehearsing the argument, and picture one small, real way to make coming back easier: a message, a seat saved, a plain hello. You don't have to send anything; just let the welcome be ready.

wordCard.voice: Coming back after a lapse. In the Sikh code, one who breaks rehat comes before the five, accepts a penance, and starts fresh. In the story of Muktsar, the Guru tears up the letter that said goodbye. Today's word.

orig.note: Punjabi: a disclaimer, a written giving-up of a claim; the letter the men signed.

carryVoice: Your line: you can return. The Guru tore the letter. A week ends with an open door.
